news.2026-10-26-libye-accord-maritime-tu: Eastern Libya approves a maritime deal with Turkey, and Greece calls it void
On 20 October, the parliament of eastern Libya unanimously approved the 2019 agreement drawing a maritime border between Libya and Turkey. Athens, Nicosia and Brussels object.

On 20 October, the House of Representatives, the parliament based in eastern Libya and close to Marshal Khalifa Haftar, unanimously approved the agreement signed in November 2019 between Turkey and Libya's former Tripoli government; it also repealed two 2020 resolutions that had rejected it [1][2].

Greece considers the deal void, since Turkey and Libya have no coasts that face or touch each other and it ignores the Greek islands lying between them; Cyprus calls it "illegal, null and void", and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says it infringes the rights of third states [1][2][3].
Turkey welcomes the decision. According to the trade press, Benghazi's approval could open the way for Turkish oil and gas drilling east of Crete [1][4].
Key point: a vote by a Libyan parliament can move a border at sea, and so decide who has the right to drill for gas in the Mediterranean [1][4].

This agreement had never been validated by eastern Libya, the rival of the Tripoli government, which is close to Ankara. By ratifying it, Benghazi moves closer to Turkey. Greece and Egypt, for their part, signed a competing agreement on their maritime economic zones in 2020, which Turkey rejects [1]. Each side draws its border to its own advantage, and what is really at stake is the future gas fields.
Eastern Mediterranean gas matters to Europe, which wants to depend less on Russia. If these waters become a legal battleground, drilling and pipeline projects may be delayed.

news.2026-10-26-roumanie-gouvernement-ni: Romania gets a government back after six months of crisis, and a big deficit to fix
Luca Niculescu, a diplomat with no party, became Prime Minister on 20 October. His team is a minority government and must first tackle the budget deficit.
On 20 October, the Romanian parliament confirmed Luca Niculescu, an independent diplomat, as Prime Minister; his 18-minister government was sworn in before President Nicușor Dan [1][2].

The country had only had a caretaker government for almost six months, since Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan was ousted by a no-confidence vote in May; Niculescu is the president's fourth choice, after three others failed [1][2].

The Social Democratic Party (PSD) holds 11 posts, seven ministers are independents, and the Finance Ministry goes to Alexandru Nazare. The government is a minority one, backed for six months by several parties, and the budget deficit is at the top of its priorities [1][2]. On energy, the country aims for 90% gas storage for the winter (87% today) and could help neighbouring Moldova in case of shortages [3].
Key point: Romania, without a stable government since May, must now correct a deficit among the heaviest in the European Union [1][2].

A country without a government cannot pass a budget or launch reforms, which worries lenders and businesses. This end to the crisis is reassuring, but support for the government is only promised for six months [2]. Winter is coming too: the state plans measures from 1 November to 31 March and can support Moldova with gas and electricity [3].
Romania is a trading partner and home to many French companies. A budget that slips weighs on its currency and on the economy of the whole region.

news.2026-10-26-zimbabwe-lithium-interdi: Zimbabwe refuses to postpone its ban on raw lithium exports
Harare is keeping the halt on exports of unrefined lithium for January 2027. The country wants batteries made at home, not just its mines feeding China.

On 9 October, Zimbabwe's government said there was no reason to delay the ban on exporting lithium as concentrate, planned for January 2027; Information Minister Nick Mangwana believes miners have had enough time to prepare to process it locally [1].
Since February 2026, the country has already suspended all exports of raw minerals and lithium concentrates, officially to control fraudulent practices in exports [2].
Mineral exports sold through the state marketing body more than doubled over the first nine months of 2026, to 4.73 billion dollars [3].
Key point: Zimbabwe, one of Africa's big lithium producers, wants to keep on its soil the part that earns the most [1][4].

Lithium concentrate is an enriched rock, sold cheaply to foreign factories that extract the product used in batteries. By banning its export, Harare forces companies to build refineries at home. The risk: if they are not ready in January, sales may stop and mines may slow down [1][4].
Lithium goes into the batteries of electric cars and phones. When a producing country tightens its rules, world supply can tighten and make batteries more expensive in the medium term.

news.2026-10-26-chili-lithium-appels-off: Chile wants to more than double its lithium by betting on private companies
Chile's mining minister announces five new tenders for lithium projects in 2027. The goal: to go from about 300,000 to 700,000 tonnes a year.
During London Metal Exchange Week (LME Week), Chile's mining minister, Daniel Mas, announced that Chile plans to open tenders for about five new lithium projects in 2027 [1].

These projects could lift the country's output from about 300,000 tonnes a year to 700,000 tonnes within five to ten years; five projects awaiting approval will be run entirely by private companies, and the state hopes to approve them in early 2027 [1].

Chile, Argentina, Bolivia and Peru also want to negotiate their lithium and copper as a bloc rather than each on its own; the text signed in late August in Santiago does not yet create an alliance [2].
Key point: Chile, already a lithium giant, wants to more than double its output by giving private companies more room [1].

Lithium is the battery metal. The country depends heavily on its copper, and lithium is its second bet. More tenders means more competition among buyers, but also more pressure on the water of the salt flats, the salt deserts from which brine is pumped [1]. Bringing four neighbours together as a bloc would give them weight on prices, but they are also competitors [2].
If lithium output doubles, the price of electric car batteries may fall over time. But that first depends on the permits, which are still to be obtained.

news.2026-10-26-pacifique-japon-micrones: Pacific: Japan hosts Micronesia while Australia settles into Papua New Guinea
On 26 October, Tokyo hosted Micronesia's president, and Canberra said it is already applying its defence treaty with Papua New Guinea. Major powers are competing for influence in the Pacific.

On 26 October in Tokyo, Japan's Prime Minister and the President of the Federated States of Micronesia reaffirmed Pacific unity and agreed to prepare the next Japan–Pacific Islands summit (PALM 11), planned for Yokohama next summer [1].

The same day, Australia said it is already implementing the Pukpuk mutual defence treaty signed with Papua New Guinea: police training, support for the justice system and recruitment of Papua New Guineans into the Australian army [1].
These announcements come as a French researcher warns of Chinese activity in Micronesia, French Polynesia, New Caledonia and Guam, while judging the military risk to be low [2].
Key point: tiny Pacific states, rich in their huge fishing zones, are courted by Japan, Australia and China [1][2].

These countries have few inhabitants but control vast sea areas, with their fish and undersea cables. Whoever has friends there gains votes in international bodies and friendly ports for their ships [1][2].
What is at stake in the Pacific concerns fishing (tuna) and the cables that carry our data. Rivalry between major powers weighs on Asia's trade routes.

news.2026-10-26-etats-unis-interdit-deep: Washington bans DeepSeek, the Chinese AI, from all its civilian agencies
The Department of Homeland Security has ordered civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek products and stop buying them, fearing data transfers to China.

The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ordered civilian federal agencies to remove DeepSeek from their systems and stop buying it, as well as tools from other companies that incorporate it; the order is based on a 2018 law on supply chain security [1][2][3].
DHS cites the risk that employees or contractors send sensitive data to China, and mentions malware and flaws in the DeepSeek iPhone app [1][3].

The order covers neither private companies nor individuals; according to one outlet, the military and intelligence services are exempt, and exceptions can be requested within 60 days [1]. Sources differ on the signing date, late July, the order having been made public in recent days [1][3].
Key point: the United States is closing its government's access to a Chinese AI that made a name for itself by rivalling American models [1][2].

AI software reads what you type into it. If the text goes to servers in a rival country, secrets can leak. Washington is here applying to AI the method already used for Chinese telecom equipment [1][3]. The Commerce Department, New York, Tennessee and Virginia had already imposed narrower bans [1].

These rules do not apply to you, but they show that AI is becoming a battleground between China and the United States, as chips have been. It may limit the AI products that companies are allowed to use.

news.2026-10-26-liban-israel-tampa-negoc: Lebanon and Israel negotiate in Tampa: a ceasefire on one side, Hezbollah's disarmament on the other
Lebanese and Israeli delegations met in the United States on 20 October. Beirut wants the strikes to stop; Israel wants to see the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah.

A Lebanese military delegation was due to press on 20 October in Tampa, Florida, a demand to end Israeli attacks, at a three-way meeting with the United States; a US source describes a "technical" meeting on 20 and 21 October [1][2].
Beirut wants a ceasefire commitment and a better verification mechanism, tied to a pilot zone where the Lebanese army would deploy [1].

Under the US-defined framework, Lebanon must disarm Hezbollah and Israel withdraw gradually; Hezbollah refuses to disarm as long as the Israeli army stays, and Israel keeps striking southern Lebanon [1]. The sources consulted did not yet give the results of the meeting.
Key point: each side wants the other to move first, and the Tampa meeting does not say who will give way [1].

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly said Israel would push the Lebanese army to prove, in two pilot zones, that it can remove the Hezbollah threat, failing which Israel would act itself [1]. Without a deal, the strikes continue, and the country, already in crisis, can neither rebuild nor attract investors.
Lebanon is a French-speaking country close to France. Its stability matters for energy prices in the Mediterranean and for refugees who may arrive in Europe.
